# Design Principles {#sec-appendix-b-design-principles}

The book uses design principles at two levels. Eight core principles form the
small set a reader can carry into an unfamiliar architecture problem. The
chapter principles apply those cores to formulation, data, methods, tools,
verification, execution, transfer, evaluation, and responsibility. A chapter
may earn two principles when it resolves two different engineering choices
with different failures and review artifacts.

A principle is more than its title. Each core principle below names the failure
it predicts, the question that makes it inspectable, and the boundary that
keeps it from becoming an absolute rule.

## Core Principles

### 1. Make the architecture decision executable

**Failure prediction.** A method optimizes a convenient artifact because the
workload, software behavior, credible alternatives, physical constraints, and
acceptance checks needed for the architecture decision remain implicit.

**Review question.** What choice is being made, under which conditions, and
what observation would distinguish the alternatives?

**Boundary.** Exploration may begin before the decision is fully executable,
and some architectural obligations may remain qualitative. Those obligations
must stay visible, and exploratory output cannot support commitment until the
comparison and evidence path are explicit. Here, *executable* means that the
decision can be carried into tools and checked. It does not mean reducing
architectural judgment to one runnable artifact or metric.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-moonshot expands a compact request into a real
architecture decision. @sec-what-architect-owns returns to the framing, abstraction, and
cross-layer judgment that keep the decision coherent.

### 2. Follow the bottleneck, not the novelty

**Failure prediction.** A new method speeds candidate construction while
simulation, implementation, verification, or review still determines the time
and cost of reaching a supported decision. The apparent gain merely moves work
or risk elsewhere.

**Review question.** What work currently blocks the next supported decision,
and where will the limiting work move if this stage becomes faster?

**Boundary.** Capability research may pursue a novel method before it improves
the current workflow, provided that capability discovery is the stated goal.
For a workflow-improvement claim, count the complete path and the next
bottleneck, including human and machine cost.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales diagnoses the work
limiting architecture progress. @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization
uses that diagnosis to choose the smallest sufficient approach.

### 3. Preserve decision-critical meaning across every transformation

**Failure prediction.** A representation, translation, wrapper, retry, or
parser preserves an artifact's name and provenance while erasing a required
relationship or silently changing the design being evaluated. Later checks
then qualify evidence for the wrong candidate or for an abstraction that
cannot express the property under decision.

**Review question.** What must remain true as the design crosses this boundary,
and how will a reviewer determine that the transformation preserved it?

**Boundary.** An abstraction may omit detail that does not affect the current
decision, and a wrapper may change syntax without changing meaning. The
omission and equivalence obligation must be explicit. A meaning-changing
transformation creates a new candidate or requires the affected claims to be
re-established. Complete provenance cannot compensate for lost design meaning.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-data-representations-world-models chooses
representations by the properties the architecture decision must preserve.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces applies the same rule to tool
translation, execution, and returned artifacts.

### 4. Every result carries its conditions

**Failure prediction.** A valid local result becomes false evidence after its
design, workload, software, tool path, process condition, operating envelope,
or neighboring component changes.

**Review question.** Under exactly which conditions does this result apply,
and can another reviewer recover them and the check that qualified the result?

**Boundary.** Conditions may travel through a durable reference to an
authoritative record rather than being copied into every artifact. Record the
conditions that affect applicability, not metadata for its own sake. Reusing a
component does not reuse its conclusion when a relevant condition changes. For
a learned result, applicable conditions include the support of its training or
feedback data, representation choices and information loss, model or policy
state, retrieval state when used, and the uncertainty attached to the result.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-data-representations-world-models binds
observations to the conditions that give them meaning.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces preserves runtime identity and
lineage. @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack determines what remains applicable
after the target changes.

### 5. Different failures require different repairs

**Failure prediction.** A malformed candidate, invalid execution, misleading
measurement, unsupported interpretation, and unsafe commitment all trigger the
same retry or regeneration step. The workflow changes the wrong thing, hides
the cause, and corrupts later results.

**Review question.** What property failed, where was the failure introduced,
and which part of the work can remove its cause?

**Boundary.** The rule separates questions, outputs, and repair paths rather
than people or organizations. One person or system may perform several
responsibilities, and several symptoms may share a common repair when the
evidence supports that diagnosis.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-architecture-20-ontology separates lifecycle
responsibilities by their questions, failures, and repairs.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces contains execution failures
inside recoverable tool boundaries. @sec-feedback-verification-trust routes
qualified results to the next eligible technical action.

### 6. Stronger claims require stronger checks

**Failure prediction.** A proxy, prediction, simulation, or pass label is
treated as support for a broader implementation or signoff claim than it can
falsify. The opposite failure occurs when signoff-strength checks become a
prerequisite for every reversible exploration.

**Review question.** Could this check falsify the claim at its stated scope and
consequence?

**Boundary.** Cheap checks may guide reversible exploration when their limits
remain explicit. As the claim broadens or its consequences increase, strengthen
the check through the dimensions relevant to its failure modes. These may
include fidelity and coverage, calibration and uncertainty, support and shift
analysis, hard or negative cases, contamination controls, independence from
adaptive search, adversarial pressure, and adequate statistical power.
Falsifiability is necessary but not sufficient. Verification throughput remains
a bottleneck question under Principle 2, not a reason to weaken a consequential
claim.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-moonshot separates artifacts from architecture
results. @sec-feedback-verification-trust matches checks to claims and
qualifies the resulting action. @sec-running-the-loop stops at the limit of its
checked record. @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect keeps decisive evaluation
checks outside the system being evaluated.

### 7. Judge the architecture before crediting the assistance

**Failure prediction.** A good candidate is credited to AI without a credible
alternative or attribution test, or a faster workflow is allowed to justify an
inferior architecture.

**Review question.** Did the architecture improve under matched conditions,
and did the assistance cause that improvement at complete human and machine
cost within a stated accounting boundary?

**Boundary.** Exploratory work may leave attribution unresolved when it states
that limit. A claim of improvement requires separate judgments of architecture
quality, contribution, total cost, and robustness rather than one favorable
score. The accounting boundary must be symmetric and decision-relevant across
the alternatives. It includes differential setup, data, adaptation,
integration, tools, verification, human review, recovery, and amortized reuse
cost that could change the adoption decision.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-moonshot introduces separate tests for the
architecture result and the complete approach. @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect owns the matched
evaluation needed to attribute value to the assistance.

### 8. Delegate technical work, not architectural accountability

**Failure prediction.** Automation changes RTL, constraints, tool state, or a
recommendation while no named authority owns commitment, residual risk,
monitoring, or reopening after conditions change.

**Review question.** What may the automated system change, within which
permission, isolation, observation, and recovery boundaries, and who owns the
architecture commitment?

**Boundary.** Routine and reversible actions may be automated inside an
approved scope. The named authority must be technically qualified and
institutionally empowered to stop, commit, or reopen the work, with an
accountable organization able to support those decisions. The owner need not
repeat delegated work, but must be able to inspect its basis, accept its
consequences, and obtain the monitoring and recovery resources the commitment
requires.

**Chapter applications.** @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces bounds
and contains automated tool action. @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect preserves
evaluator control over decisive checks. @sec-what-architect-owns defines the
architect's technical role, commitment authority, and continuing accountability.

## Chapter Applications

The core principles recur because different stages expose different versions
of the same engineering tension. The chapter principle states the operational
rule earned at that stage.

| Chapter | Chapter principle | Core principle |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-moonshot | Treat the request as the beginning, not the specification. | 1 |
| @sec-moonshot | Treat artifacts as inputs to judgment, not architecture results. | 6 |
| @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales | Improve the work that limits the decision. | 2 |
| @sec-architecture-20-ontology | Separate responsibilities when failures need different repairs. | 5 |
| @sec-data-representations-world-models | Keep every observation tied to the conditions that produced it. | 4 |
| @sec-data-representations-world-models | Choose representations by what the decision must preserve. | 3 |
| @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | Choose the smallest sufficient approach. | 2 |
| @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | Tool mechanics must not change the design being evaluated. | 3, 4 |
| @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | Automate tool actions only inside a recoverable boundary. | 5, 8 |
| @sec-feedback-verification-trust | Stronger claims require stronger checks. | 6 |
| @sec-feedback-verification-trust | Let only qualified results drive the next architecture action. | 5, 6 |
| @sec-running-the-loop | Claim only what the checked record supports. | 4, 6 |
| @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack | Transfer components, not conclusions. | 4 |
| @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect | Judge the architecture before crediting the assistance. | 7 |
| @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect | Keep the decisive evaluation checks outside the system under test. | 6, 8 |
| @sec-what-architect-owns | Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends. | 1, 8 |
| @sec-what-architect-owns | Delegate technical work, not architectural accountability. | 8 |

The chapter principles are not seventeen competing fundamentals. They are the
local forms in which the eight core principles become inspectable during real
architecture work.
